# Natural Coordinatizations of Delzant Spaces

## Overview

This note describes the natural coordinatizations of a Delzant space defined as a reduced phase space and provides explicit formulas for the coordinate transformations between them. Delzant spaces admit two complementary descriptions—one arising from symplectic reduction and another from the theory of toric varieties—and understanding how these descriptions relate to one another is essential for working effectively within either framework. Our aim is to make these relationships precise and computationally accessible.

## Maximal Coordinatizations at Fixed Points

The central construction concerns the fixed points of the torus action on the Delzant polytope. For each such fixed point, there exists a maximal coordinatization of an open cell in the Delzant space that contains that fixed point. These coordinatizations are natural in the sense that they arise directly from the geometry of the polytope and the associated torus action, and each provides a chart in which the local structure of the Delzant space can be described explicitly.

A key observation is that this open cell coincides exactly with the domain of one of the natural coordinatizations of the Delzant space when the latter is viewed as a toric variety. In other words, the coordinate neighborhoods obtained from the reduced phase space perspective are precisely those that appear in the standard atlas of the toric variety. This correspondence establishes a direct bridge between the symplectic and algebraic-geometric viewpoints.

## Explicit Coordinate Transformations

To make this correspondence fully concrete, we give an explicit formula expressing the toric variety coordinates in terms of the reduced phase space coordinates. This formula allows one to pass directly between the two descriptions of the Delzant space, translating computations carried out in one framework into the other without ambiguity. Such explicit transformations are valuable both for theoretical purposes and for concrete calculations, as they remove any reliance on abstract identification between the two constructions.

## Consequences and Applications

Working within these maximal coordinate neighborhoods yields several benefits. In particular, considerations carried out in these charts lead to simple proofs of basic facts about the Delzant space, replacing more abstract arguments with direct local computations. Moreover, this approach helps make the presentation more self-contained, since many of the fundamental properties of Delzant spaces can be established directly from the explicit coordinatizations rather than being imported from external results. In this way, the coordinate-based perspective serves both as a computational tool and as a foundation for a coherent and largely self-contained treatment of the subject.

# Coordinatizations of Delzant Spaces

## Introduction

The Delzant space stands as one of the most elegant constructions in modern symplectic geometry, occupying a distinctive position at the intersection of two major mathematical traditions. On one hand, it arises naturally within symplectic geometry as a reduced phase space—the outcome of applying symplectic reduction to a Hamiltonian torus action. On the other hand, the very same object emerges from complex algebraic geometry as a toric variety, a class of spaces defined by their combinatorial data and their intimate relationship with algebraic tori. This note undertakes a careful examination of the natural coordinate systems that a Delzant space inherits when viewed through these two distinct lenses, and it establishes the precise dictionary that translates between them.

## Coordinatizations from the Symplectic Perspective

When we regard a Delzant space as a reduced phase space, its coordinatizations arise organically from the symplectic reduction procedure. The construction begins with a convex polytope—the Delzant polytope—whose combinatorial structure encodes all the essential geometric information. From this starting point, one derives explicit local coordinate systems that parametrize the space near its various regions.

A central theme of this note is the systematic derivation of the explicit formulas governing the transformations between these different coordinatizations. Rather than treating these coordinate changes abstractly, we compute them directly, obtaining concrete expressions that reveal how the various natural charts fit together to cover the entire space. These transformation formulas serve as the technical backbone for the analysis that follows.

## The Bridge to Toric Variety Coordinates

Parallel to the symplectic coordinatizations stand the coordinates that the Delzant space inherits as a toric variety in complex algebraic geometry. These arise from the algebraic-geometric structure, reflecting the way in which the toric variety is assembled from affine pieces indexed by the combinatorial data of the fan associated with the polytope.

One of the principal contributions of this note is to relate the symplectic coordinatizations explicitly to these toric variety coordinates. By establishing precise formulas connecting the two families of coordinate systems, we make transparent the sense in which the reduced phase space and the toric variety are genuinely the same object, described in two different mathematical languages. This correspondence is not merely a qualitative statement of equivalence; it is realized through explicit change-of-coordinate maps.

## Torus Fixed Points and Maximal Coordinatizations

A particularly clean organizing principle emerges from the action of the torus on the Delzant space. Each fixed point of this torus action corresponds combinatorially to a vertex of the Delzant polytope. What we find is that each such fixed point gives rise to a maximal coordinatization of an open cell within the space. In other words, the fixed points of the torus action are precisely the anchors around which the most extensive natural coordinate neighborhoods are organized.

These maximal coordinatizations cover open cells whose union constitutes the full Delzant space, so that the collection of charts indexed by the fixed points provides a complete atlas. The maximality of each coordinatization means that within each of these neighborhoods, one has the largest possible domain on which a single natural coordinate system remains valid, offering an especially convenient setting for local computations.

## Applications: Simple Proofs from Both Perspectives

Having assembled this framework of coordinatizations, we turn to its utility. By carrying out analysis within these maximal coordinate neighborhoods, we are able to give simple, transparent proofs of a number of basic facts about the Delzant space. Because the maximal charts are both explicit and expansive, arguments that might otherwise require abstract machinery become accessible through direct local calculation.

Crucially, these proofs illuminate the Delzant space from both of its incarnations. We recover basic structural facts as they appear from the symplectic-geometric standpoint, and we likewise establish corresponding facts as they arise in the algebraic-geometric setting of toric varieties. In this way, the coordinatizations serve as a common tool that speaks to both communities, and the parallel treatment underscores the unity of the two perspectives.

This application serves a dual purpose. First, it demonstrates a first practical use of the coordinatizations we have developed, showing that they are not merely of formal interest but genuinely facilitate mathematical work. Second, by supplying self-contained proofs of the foundational facts, it renders the overall presentation more complete and independent, allowing the reader to appreciate the essential features of the Delzant space without recourse to external results. Taken together, these contributions offer a coherent account of how the natural coordinate systems on a Delzant space can be understood, related, and put to work.

# The Delzant Theorem in Symplectic Geometry

The Delzant theorem stands as one of the most elegant results in the study of toric symplectic manifolds, establishing a remarkable bridge between geometry and combinatorics. Named after the mathematician Thomas Delzant, who proved it in 1988, this theorem provides a complete classification of compact toric symplectic manifolds in terms of simple combinatorial objects known as Delzant polytopes.

## Understanding the Core Idea

**For** a symplectic manifold of dimension 2n equipped with an effective Hamiltonian action of an n-dimensional torus, the image of the moment map turns out to be a convex polytope. Delzant discovered that not every polytope can arise this way. Instead, the polytopes must satisfy specific conditions—they must be *simple*, *rational*, and *smooth*. Such polytopes are precisely the objects we now call Delzant polytopes.

**This** correspondence works in both directions, which is what makes it so powerful. Given any Delzant polytope, one can construct a unique toric symplectic manifold whose moment map image reproduces that exact polytope. Conversely, every compact toric symplectic manifold gives rise to a Delzant polytope through its moment map.

## Why It Matters

The significance of Delzant's result lies in its reduction of a difficult geometric classification problem to a manageable combinatorial one. **For** researchers working in symplectic topology, algebraic geometry, and mathematical physics, this means that questions about complicated manifolds can often be translated into questions about polytopes—objects that are far easier to visualize and manipulate.

**This** framework has influenced numerous areas of modern mathematics, from mirror symmetry to the study of integrable systems. The interplay between the combinatorial data of the polytope and the rich geometry of the manifold continues to inspire new research directions today.

In summary, the Delzant theorem exemplifies the deep and beautiful connections that unify seemingly distinct branches of mathematics.

# Natural Coordinatizations of Delzant Spaces via Torus Fixed Points

## Abstract

Let $\Delta \subset \mathfrak{t}^*$ be a Delzant polytope in the dual of the Lie algebra of a compact torus $T \cong (S^1)^n$, and let $(M_\Delta, \omega, \mu)$ denote the associated symplectic toric manifold furnished by the Delzant construction as a symplectic quotient of $\mathbb{C}^d$. We develop a systematic theory of natural coordinatizations of $M_\Delta$ organized around the fixed points of the Hamiltonian $T$-action, which correspond bijectively to the vertices of $\Delta$. For each vertex $v$, the local structure of the polytope—encoded by the primitive inward normal vectors of the $n$ facets meeting at $v$—determines a canonical unimodular chart in which the symplectic form assumes Darboux form and the moment map is expressed explicitly in action-angle-type coordinates.

Our central result establishes that these fixed points sit at the center of **open dense cells**, each equivariantly symplectomorphic to a standard model $(\mathbb{C}^n, \omega_{\mathrm{std}})$ with linear torus action, whose complement has measure zero. We show that the transition functions between overlapping cells are governed by the combinatorics of the polytope's edges and the $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{Z})$ data relating adjacent vertices. This yields an atlas that is simultaneously compatible with the symplectic, complex, and torus-invariant structures, thereby providing an intrinsic bridge between the polytopal combinatorics and the smooth symplectic geometry.

As applications, we furnish streamlined, coordinate-based proofs of several foundational results in the theory. First, we recover the **Delzant classification theorem**, demonstrating that the fixed-point cell decomposition reconstructs $M_\Delta$ uniquely up to equivariant symplectomorphism from $\Delta$ alone. Second, we give a transparent derivation of the **Duistermaat–Heckman theorem**, computing the pushforward of the Liouville measure under $\mu$ by localizing to the fixed-point charts and exhibiting the piecewise-polynomial density directly from the local coordinate volumes. Third, we obtain a clean proof of the **convexity (Atiyah–Guillemin–Sternberg) theorem** in the toric setting, with the image $\mu(M_\Delta) = \Delta$ emerging from the local moment-map normal forms and connectedness of fibers. Finally, we indicate how the cell structure computes the equivariant cohomology and the **ABBV localization formula**, with contributions indexed by vertices weighted by the products of the edge weights emanating from each fixed point.

**Keywords:** Delzant polytope, symplectic toric manifold, moment map, torus fixed points, Darboux coordinates, Duistermaat–Heckman measure, equivariant localization, convexity theorem.

**MSC 2020:** 53D20, 53D05, 14M25, 37J35.
